body:
From a hazardous event to a disaster

An industrial accident, an infectious-disease outbreak and a dam failure may appear unrelated. However, all 3 can threaten human life, damage property, interrupt essential services and require coordinated action by several authorities. Disaster management seeks to prevent such events where possible, reduce their consequences and prepare communities to respond safely.

A hazard is a potentially damaging event, substance or condition. Exposure refers to people, property, infrastructure or activities located where the hazard may cause harm. Vulnerability describes the conditions that make exposed people or systems more susceptible to damage. These include weak infrastructure, inadequate warning arrangements, limited healthcare access and lack of resources to respond.

Disaster risk arises from the interaction of a hazard with exposure and vulnerability. A hazardous chemical stored in a well-managed facility is not itself a disaster. If containment fails, the consequences depend on the material involved, the quantity released, the people exposed and the effectiveness of protective measures.

How the 3 hazard groups differ

Hazard groupPrincipal dangerMain risk-reduction approach
Industrial and chemicalToxic release, fire, explosion or contaminationProcess safety, containment, safe siting and emergency planning
BiologicalInfectious disease spreading through a populationSurveillance, prevention, healthcare capacity and public communication
Dam and infrastructureStructural or operational failure, sudden flooding and service disruptionInspection, maintenance, monitoring and downstream warning

Industrial accidents and dam failures can develop very rapidly. Infectious diseases may spread through chains of transmission over days or weeks, although some outbreaks also demand an immediate response. The correct warning and protective action therefore depend on the nature of the hazard.

Prevention, preparedness and response

Prevention addresses the causes of a hazardous event, such as defective industrial equipment or unsafe dam conditions. Mitigation reduces the likely damage, for example by restricting vulnerable development near hazardous installations. Preparedness establishes warning systems, plans, trained personnel and public awareness before an emergency. Response protects life and meets urgent needs when an incident occurs. Recovery restores services and livelihoods while seeking to reduce future risk.

One hazard can trigger another

A natural event may cause a technological accident. For example, flooding may damage an industrial installation and release stored hazardous material. Such a combination is often called a natural hazard-triggered technological accident. Similarly, a major flood may damage roads, electricity supply and drinking-water systems, making rescue and recovery more difficult.

Prelims focus

  • A hazard is a potential source of harm; a disaster occurs when its consequences seriously disrupt a community or society.
  • Exposure concerns the people and assets in harm's way; vulnerability concerns their susceptibility to damage.
  • Prevention addresses causes, while preparedness establishes the ability to respond.
  • Industrial, biological and dam emergencies may all interrupt essential services.
  • Trap: A hazardous installation does not automatically constitute a disaster.

[Sources: National Disaster Management Authority, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Chemical Disasters (Industrial), 2007, chapters 1 and 4; World Health Organization, One Health, fact sheet dated 8 May 2026; Dam Safety Act, 2021, sections 28, 35 and 36. Online sources accessed 2 November 2026.]

title: Understanding Industrial, Biological and Dam-Related Disaster Risks

body:
What is an industrial or chemical disaster?

An industrial disaster is a serious accident arising from industrial activities that causes substantial harm or disruption. A chemical disaster involves the accidental release or harmful effects of hazardous chemicals during their manufacture, processing, storage, handling or transportation.

Not every industrial accident involves chemicals. Mechanical failures and major fires may also cause industrial disasters. Conversely, a hazardous chemical accident may occur outside a factory, such as during transportation or at an isolated storage facility.

Different properties create different hazards

PropertyMeaningIllustrative danger
ToxicCan injure living organisms through harmful exposureInhalation of a toxic gas
FlammableCan ignite under suitable conditionsFire involving a fuel or solvent
ExplosiveCan release energy rapidly under particular conditionsBlast and flying debris
CorrosiveCan damage tissues or materials through chemical actionChemical burns or equipment deterioration
ReactiveMay undergo dangerous reactions under incompatible conditionsUncontrolled heat, pressure or hazardous products

A chemical may possess more than 1 hazardous property. The terms toxic, flammable and corrosive are not interchangeable: they describe different ways in which a substance can cause harm.

The risk also depends on how exposure occurs. People may be harmed by inhaling contaminated air, contacting a hazardous substance or consuming contaminated food or water. A fire or explosion may injure people through heat, pressure and debris even without direct contact with a toxic chemical.

How accidents develop

Industrial chemicals are normally kept within equipment, pipelines and containers. A loss of containment occurs when a substance escapes from the equipment intended to hold it. Contributing factors may include corrosion, equipment deterioration, unsafe operations, human error, inadequate maintenance or damage caused by a natural hazard.

The consequences depend on the substance and circumstances. A release might remain limited, cause harmful exposure, ignite or contribute to a wider accident. Fire can damage nearby equipment and trigger further releases. This is called a domino effect when an initial accident sets off additional accidents.

Process safety prevents major accidents

Process safety concerns the prevention of major releases of hazardous substances and the control of serious industrial accident risks. It differs from the narrower concern of preventing individual workplace injuries, although both are important.

Process safety relies on several complementary safeguards:

  • Hazard identification: Recognising dangerous substances, processes and possible failure conditions.
  • Safe design and containment: Using suitable equipment and protective arrangements to prevent uncontrolled releases.
  • Inspection and maintenance: Detecting deterioration and correcting faults before they cause serious failures.
  • Operating discipline and training: Ensuring that workers understand the hazards and follow approved safety arrangements.
  • Monitoring and alarms: Recognising abnormal conditions so that authorised personnel can act.
  • Learning from incidents: Investigating accidents and near misses to prevent recurrence.

A near miss is an event that could have caused harm but did not produce the feared consequence. Reporting it can reveal a weakness before a major accident occurs.

Process safety seeks to prevent or control a major hazardous event. Emergency response addresses the consequences when prevention is insufficient. A response plan cannot substitute for safe plant operation.

Prelims focus

  • Chemical hazards can arise during manufacture, storage, handling and transportation.
  • Toxicity concerns harmful exposure; flammability concerns the capacity to ignite.
  • Loss of containment means the unintended escape of a substance from its intended enclosure.
  • A domino effect occurs when an initial accident triggers additional accidents.
  • Process safety includes hazard identification, maintenance, monitoring, training and incident learning.
  • Trap: A chemical need not be flammable to cause a serious chemical disaster.

[Sources: National Disaster Management Authority, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Chemical Disasters (Industrial), 2007, chapters 1, 3 and 4; Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, Chemical and Industrial Disaster, sections on causative factors and industrial vulnerability. Online sources accessed 2 November 2026.]

title: Industrial and Chemical Disasters: Hazardous Materials and Process Safety

body:
Why emergency plans are needed

Even a well-managed industrial facility cannot assume that a major accident is impossible. An emergency plan identifies likely accident scenarios, clarifies responsibilities, establishes communication arrangements and prepares people to act without avoidable delay.

For hazardous industrial activities covered by the relevant rules, India distinguishes between on-site and off-site emergency planning. The dividing consideration is whether the response concerns the industrial site itself or people and areas outside it.

On-site and off-site plans are not the same

FeatureOn-site emergency planOff-site emergency plan
Primary responsibilityIndustrial occupierConcerned authority, ordinarily the District Collector or designated District Emergency Authority
Main area of concernWorkers, installations and operations within the siteNearby residents, roads, public services and areas beyond the site
Main arrangementsInternal alerts, designated personnel, incident control and coordinationPublic warning, interagency coordination, shelter or evacuation arrangements and relief
Legal basisRule 13 of the MSIHC Rules, 1989Rule 14 of the MSIHC Rules, 1989

The occupier is the person or organisation having control over the industrial activity as defined by the applicable rules. The occupier must provide relevant hazard information to the authority preparing the off-site plan. The authority prepares that plan in consultation with the occupier and other necessary persons.

Under the specified provisions of the Manufacture, Storage and Import of Hazardous Chemicals Rules, 1989, the occupier must conduct an on-site mock drill every 6 months. The concerned authority must ensure rehearsal of the off-site plan at least once in a calendar year. These are distinct requirements, not interchangeable frequencies.

How industrial and district planning connect

A serious leak may first be detected inside a facility. The occupier's emergency organisation assesses and reports the situation through established channels. When the public may be affected, the designated authorities coordinate warnings, public protection and assistance from the relevant emergency services. The industrial organisation remains responsible for its own obligations; an off-site plan does not transfer all responsibility away from it.

Land-use buffers reduce exposure

Land-use planning considers whether factories, warehouses, housing, schools, hospitals and other developments are located appropriately in relation to known hazards. A buffer zone is an area of separation or controlled land use intended to reduce exposure between a hazardous activity and vulnerable development.

The appropriate separation depends on the substance, possible accident scenarios, surrounding population, geography and other local conditions. There is no single universal buffer distance that makes every hazardous installation safe. A buffer also does not replace process safety or emergency planning.

Standard precautions for the public

People living near a hazardous installation should know the official warning channels, available evacuation routes and where reliable instructions will be issued. During an actual incident, the appropriate public action depends on the substance, weather conditions and official assessment.

  • Follow instructions issued by the district administration and authorised emergency services.
  • Move away from the incident area and avoid gathering to watch the accident.
  • Follow an official direction to shelter indoors or evacuate; neither action is suitable for every chemical incident.
  • Avoid suspected contaminated water, food and exposed materials until authorities advise that they are safe.
  • Seek medical assistance when exposure or symptoms are suspected, and share verified information rather than rumours.

Public sheltering and evacuation are alternative protective measures chosen according to the incident. An instruction suitable for a particular chemical release should not be treated as a universal rule for all chemical emergencies.

Prelims focus

  • Rule 13 of the MSIHC Rules, 1989 concerns on-site emergency plans prepared by occupiers.
  • Rule 14 concerns off-site emergency plans prepared by the concerned authority.
  • On-site mock drills are required every 6 months under Rule 13.
  • Off-site plan rehearsals are required at least once per calendar year under Rule 14.
  • Land-use buffers aim to reduce the exposure of vulnerable populations.
  • Trap: The off-site emergency plan is not prepared solely by the factory occupier.

[Sources: Government of India, Manufacture, Storage and Import of Hazardous Chemicals Rules, 1989, Rules 13, 14 and 15 and Schedule 5, as amended; National Disaster Management Authority, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Chemical Disasters (Industrial), 2007, sections on on-site and off-site emergency management. Online sources accessed 2 November 2026.]
